title: Why Mapmakers Put Fake Towns on Their Maps in the 1920s — and the One That Became Real
description: Open Cul­ture read­ers may know John Green best for Crash Course, the YouTube chan­nel that teach­es every­thing you need to know about sub­j
body:
Open Cul­ture read­ers may know John Green best for Crash Course, the YouTube chan­nel that teach­es every­thing you need to know about sub­jects like world his­to­ry, U.S. his­to­ry, big his­to­ry, lit­er­a­ture, and phi­los­o­phy. Or at least it teach­es every­thing a teenage stu­dent fac­ing down the prospect of Advanced Place­ment sub­ject exams needs to know. Such view­ers have always had a decent chance of know­ing Green as the author of nov­els for young read­ers like Look­ing for Alas­ka, The Fault in Our Stars, and Paper Towns. That last takes its title from just the kind of his­tor­i­cal phe­nom­e­non that would in any case have fas­ci­nat­ed Green, in his capac­i­ty as a vlog­ger, enough to inspire a video: the whol­ly fic­tion­al set­tle­ments cre­at­ed by map­mak­ers in order to expose car­to­graph­ic pla­gia­rists.

Green dis­cuss­es one such paper town in the episode of Vlog­broth­ers, the long-run­ning chan­nel Green runs with his broth­er Hank, at the top of the post. Agloe, New York, an upstate ham­let in Colch­ester, Delaware Coun­ty, was fab­ri­cat­ed in the nine­teen-twen­ties by car­tog­ra­ph­er Otto G. Lind­berg and his assis­tant Ernest Alpers, who’d been com­mis­sioned to make maps for the gas-sta­tion chain Esso.
Map­mak­ers (like Lind­berg and Alpers) have guard­ed against pla­gia­rism by insert­ing “paper towns” — invent­ed streets, land­marks, or oth­er fea­tures — into their maps. The log­ic is sim­ple: two car­tog­ra­phers might eas­i­ly draw the same real town, but two car­tog­ra­phers can’t inde­pen­dent­ly dream up the same fake one. So if a rival’s map con­tains the same invent­ed place, it all but proves they copied the map.
Though intend­ed as noth­ing more than a “copy­right trap,” the name of the dot in the road, Agloe, soon man­i­fest­ed in the real world. A busi­ness named Agloe Lodge Farms appeared in 1930, and it went on to apply the name to a local fish­ing lodge it acquired. Thus was Agloe, New York brought into exis­tence, at least in the eyes of the law: by the time they were chal­lenged about its inclu­sion on their own maps, Rand McNal­ly could cite offi­cial coun­ty records in their defense.

In oth­er words, “a made-up name for a made-up place inad­ver­tent­ly cre­at­ed a real place that, for a time, real­ly exist­ed,” writes NPR’s Robert Krul­wich. “Rand McNal­ly, one pre­sumes, was found not guilty. Then the store closed. It isn’t there any­more. Decades passed.” At the time Krul­wich was writ­ing, in 2014, an inter­net search for Agloe, New York would still return a point where Lind­berg and Alpers had orig­i­nal­ly placed it on their map the bet­ter part of a cen­tu­ry ear­li­er. “But then, just as this sto­ry was to be pub­lished, to be extra sure, we went to Google Earth, typed in ‘Agloe’ one last time, and, whad­dya know? It isn’t there any more!” Ado­les­cent read­ers imag­in­ing them­selves run­ning away in the man­ner of Mar­go Spiegel­man will have to seek out anoth­er far­away paper town to dream about — or, more like­ly these days, a pix­el town.

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: The Top Photos in the CWAS David Malin Awards Highlight Astronomical Wonders
description: Every year, the Central West Astronomical Society (CWAS) of New South Wales celebrates AstroFest, a festival of astronomy during which amateur pho
body:
Every year, the Central West Astronomical Society (CWAS) of New South Wales celebrates AstroFest, a festival of astronomy during which amateur photographers and scientists from around the globe are invited to submit their best views of the night sky and beyond. This year, the overall prize was awarded to Stefan Buda for his tonal moonscape titled “The Lunar Apennines,” which captures a detailed view of Montes Apenninus.
Categories include Deep Sky, Solar System, Wide-Field, Nightscapes, and more, allowing photographers to contribute images of phenomena ranging from distant nebulae and spiral galaxies to the Milky Way and aurora australis, or the southern lights, shining above impressive terrestrial landscapes. A 2027 calendar featuring the winning images is available for purchase, and you can see the entire gallery of top shots on the award’s website.
Stefan Buda, “The Lunar Apennines.” Overall winner of the CWAS David Malin Award and winner of the Solar System category
Andy Campbell, “OED1 – Winged Sandals of Mercury.” Honorable mention in the Deep Sky category
Luke Tscharke, “Tasman Arc.” Honorable mention in the Nightscapes (International) category
Paul Montague, “NGC 1097 – A Barred Spiral with Jets.” Honorable mention in the Deep Sky category
Jarrod Rueff, “BRAN 56.” Honorable mention in the Deep Sky category
Luke Rasmussen, “The Wishing Tree.” Honorable mention in the Nightscapes (International) category
Andy Campbell, “The Rippling Flames – Chamaeleon III.” Winner of the Deep Sky category
Lucy Yunxi Hu, “Milky Way and Zodiacal Light.” Honorable mention in the Nightscapes (International) category
Brighton Seeley, “Zenith.” Winner of the Nightscapes (International) category

title: Reflections Dazzle in the Hyperrealistic Chrome Faces of Kip Omolade's Vivid Portraits
description: Set against uninterrupted backgrounds, the bold, metallic portraits of Kip Omolade float almost deity-like amid vibrant color. Known for his hyper
body:
Set against uninterrupted backgrounds, the bold, metallic portraits of Kip Omolade float almost deity-like amid vibrant color. Known for his hyperrealistic treatment of chrome-like visages in oil paint, the artist sometimes incorporates spray-painted elements, drawing on the graffiti culture of New York City’s subways during the 1980s and 1990s when Omolade tagged using the moniker “Kace.”
The artist also presents the mask-like faces from different vantage points, sometimes with incredible eyelashes, whether peering directly at the viewer or positioned in regal profile. Reflections are typically abstract, showing little indication of the surrounding space beyond perhaps blue skies, the sun, and local color, although the monumental “African History” is an exception.
“Diovadiova Chrome Karyn XXII”
Upon closer inspection, the whorls of “African History” reveal numerous additional faces inspired by a wide range of carved sculptures the artist observed in a long-running exhibition at The Metropolitan Museum of Art titled The African Origin of Civilization, plus other examples from art history. Within this one, larger-than-life identity is a host of time-honored traditions and creative expressions.

title: Heritage Bookbinding Elements Transform in Contemporary Sculptures by Adelene Koh
description: After visiting the New York Art Book Fair in 2011, Adelene Koh was smitten with the world of bookbinding. Her professional training commenced in J
body:
After visiting the New York Art Book Fair in 2011, Adelene Koh was smitten with the world of bookbinding. Her professional training commenced in Japan, then led her to London, and she’s now based in Taiwan, where she runs a studio called dddots. This year, Koh was one of 30 finalists for the Loewe Foundation Craft Prize, which celebrates innovation across a wide range of artisanship.
As a bookmaker and conservator, Koh draws upon the technical precision and heritage of bookmaking to create unique sculptures using paper and thread. Her work “Endless” was included in the prize’s exhibition of shortlisted artists, consisting of a kind of ouroboros-like cylinder of meticulously folded paper and edges stitched with colorful fiber. “The result is an endless loop of a book’s spine and fore-edge bound together by the English endband sewing techniques from the 18th and 19th centuries,” says a statement.

Sewn endbands are not exactly invisible, but they’re usually tucked snugly inside the cover. The thread is also not necessarily colorful, as it may be selected to blend in with the pages or other parts of the binding. For Koh, this underappreciated element becomes the highlight through vibrant combinations and rhythmic patterns. “I’m interested in bringing hidden elements of books into focus,” Koh says. “I’m drawn to the overlooked, the sidelined, the parts that quietly support everything else.”
The winner of this year’s competition is Jongjin Park, and Colossal readers may also recognize the work of finalist Xanthe Somers. See more on Koh’s Instagram.

body:
Community

            Welcome to the 348th installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Connor Czora mines the history of porcelain ceramics while teaching the next generation of potters in DC.Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.Connor Czora, Washington, DCHow long have you been working in this space?Seven years.Describe an average day in your studio.I work at District Clay Center, where I also teach. Every day, I get to the studio between 1pm and 2pm to catch up on emails before diving into my own work. Ceramics go through several stages before they’re finished: throwing/building, surface decoration, glazing, decal transfers, and gilding. Each stage can take days or weeks, so in one workday, I’ll often find myself just throwing or just applying luster. I rotate between music and audiobooks in the background.

title: V&A Storehouse Workers Vote to Strike Over “Amazon-Style” Conditions
description:
News
                Staff members allege they were “denied sufficient time during the day for toilet breaks or for drinks.”
body:
News
                Staff members allege they were “denied sufficient time during the day for toilet breaks or for drinks.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Victoria and Albert (V&A) East Storehouse, a publicly accessible museum storage site in East London (photo 14GTR via Wikimedia Commons, CC0 1.0)
    
        
            Unionized workers at the Victoria and Albert (V&A) East Storehouse, a publicly accessible museum storage site, have voted unanimously to strike over alleged "Amazon-style" working practices.On Wednesday, July 29, all of the Storehouse employees who voted in a union ballot said they would go on strike, citing being "denied sufficient time during the day for toilet breaks or for drinks," according to a press release shared by Prospect, the union that represents them. The union is demanding that the museum give employees two paid breaks per day, a request it said the museum has failed to adopt.

title: Long-Contested Guggenheim Abu Dhabi Gets Opening Date
description:
News
                Activists have called on artists to boycott the new museum, citing inhumane treatment of workers.
body:
News
                Activists have called on artists to boycott the new museum, citing inhumane treatment of workers. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Exterior of the Frank Gehry-designed Guggenheim Abu Dhabi (all images courtesy Guggenheim Abu Dhabi)
    
        
            After 20 years of delays, allegations, and recalibrations, the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation will open the doors to its Frank Gehry-designed Abu Dhabi outpost on December 11. The 30-gallery museum will join seven other cultural institutions on Saadiyat Island, including the Zayed National Museum and Berklee Abu Dhabi."The museum’s art collection is uniquely local and global, centred in the region but with works from all continents," Guggenheim Director and CEO Mariët Westermann said in a statement. She expressed that the museum will showcase the "experimental character of art since 1960," including abstractions, storytelling, painting, and moving images. In the past 16 years, the art activism group Gulf Labor Coalition (GLC) has been calling attention to abuse allegations of migrant workers and violations of local and international labor laws linked to the new museum. In 2015, an offshoot of the group called Gulf Ultra Luxury Faction (G.U.L.F.) staged a May Day occupation of the Guggenheim Museum in New York and a May 8 occupation of the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice during the Venice Biennale. On May Day 2015, members of the Gulf Ultra Luxury Faction (G.U.L.F.) unveiled a large parachute in the Guggenheim Museum rotunda with the words “Meet Workers Demands Now” (photo Benjamin Sutton/Hyperallergic)"None of the initial reasons for this action have been adequately resolved over the years, despite Gulf Labor's strident efforts, and the art world's generally sympathetic response," GLC Co-Founder Andrew Ross told Hyperallergic after this week's announcement about the December opening.The Guggenheim Museum and Foundation has not yet responded to Hyperallergic's request for comment.
